live_attach.answer_text:
You walk to one building and not the other. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. Your town has two bishops, two basilicas, two sets of hands that will say the words over you - and you choose which door to walk through, on a day that can be named, in front of people who can see which way you have gone. That choice is the entry itself, not a preliminary to it.

If you come to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was. Washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

After that you were among us. You gathered with us when we gathered. Each year, on the day one of our own died, you stood at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. You heard it the same way most of us received the words at all - aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, unable to check a single detail and there anyway.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong. What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. The bishop of Hippo's own case against us concedes it - that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

The harder question is what happened when someone wronged us and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again [[don.term.
